3D Safe Implants

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche: The medical world has been revolutionised through the help of 3D printing. Tonight we go to theatre to see how a team of experts perform miracles.

Unique Selling Point:
Through the revolutionary medical advances of safe 3D printed implants, patients are now able to leave surgery without any disfigurement of their facial features and lead a normal life.


Summary:
Summary: Six years ago Belinda Dzambo from Mayville in Durban was diagnosed with a tumour of the jawbone. Over the years it became worst and eventually spread to the entire right hand side of her face. Bleeding, severe discomfort and disfigurement of her face has left her in despair.

She was put on a waiting list at the state hospital for an operation that will remove the tumour but at the same time leave her with facial disfigurement. Reconstructive surgery after such an operation is the norm, but for Belinda this was not an option as state patients are not afforded that luxury.

Then a few weeks ago she was contacted by Dr. Vivesh Rughubar, a maxillofacial surgeon from the King Edward state hospital in Durban with the good news. Through private funding and sponsorship her life was about to change.


Further information:
We will visit Belinda at her home in Mayville where she lives with her sister, Shingi. Her two children are living in Zimbabwe with her mother as she has no means to look after them without a job. Her home language is Shona but we will converse with her through our Presenter, in Zulu.

She has told us that she lives with pain and bleeding for too long. Her condition is desperate and she is thankful that she was chosen to receive the procedure free of charge. She hopes this is going to change her life as she is embarrassed about her disfigurement. At the same time she is nervous and scared and just hope that it will be a success.

As a secondary case study 30 year old Busisiwe Masuku who lives in rural KZN will be interviewed at the hospital. This is not ideal as we do not see her home environment but her interview will be short.

Background:
In 2007 the Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) was established in Bloemfontein at the Central University of Technology (TUT) in the Free State. CRPM is considered one of the top centres in the world and the only one of its kind in the southern hemisphere. There are ten printing machines able to produce parts in titanium and a number of other materials for industries such as aerospace and architect and design and even jewelry in 3D printing.

3D printing, also called Additive Manufacturing, or AD is a process of joining materials layer upon layer until the final product or model is completed in the desired material. In this instance Belinda’s artificial jawbone was printed in titanium on the 3D printing machine to the exact specification of her facial features.

In 2012 the first successful 3d implant in South Africa was successfully executed in Pretoria. Since then more than 30 state patients have been assisted through the help of private / public partnership where the medical team and hospital foot the bill and private funding sponsors the cost of the implant. Each implant costs roughly R70 000 to produce. Through this collaboration there is new hope for state patients in South Africa.

The process involved from beginning to end is fascinating as it involves a team of experts working remotely from different corners of South Africa. In this instance, Dr, Rughubar sent CT scans of Belinda’s mandible to an engineer at the CRPM centre in Bloemfontein. This was captured through software on a computer and first printed in nylon as a test model. Due to the cost of titanium nylon is used as a dummy model. Once the team was satisfied with the fit and accuracy time was of an essence as the tumour keeps on growing and every month Belinda’s jaw area will start looking different. Two weeks prior to the operation, the final product was then printed in titanium and sent to Stellenbosch to be checked that there are no cracks in the model. From there it went to Cape Town to the Titamed centre where the product is polished and then finally treated by a radioactive material to ensure that there will be no infection in the patient after the surgery.

The advantages of 3D printed medical implants are that they are safe; save on hospital and recovery time and that the patients is able to lead a life of normality thanks to the perfect fit of the titanium printed model. Without the 3D printed implant the patient would have to undergo up to nine hours surgery, then ICU, then a lengthy recovery period. They are then sent home disfigured as reconstructive surgery is not affordable.

Besides the engineer in charge of the printing we will also interview the medical expert at the hospital performing the operation and hopefully will be allowed to film inside the theatre.

The programme will conclude with Belinda out of theatre and wheeled to her hospital bed where we will hopefully get a thumbs up from her to show that it went well.

Press Release:


3D Face Implants
Last year Belinda Dzambo was diagnosed with a tumour of the jawbone, leaving her swollen, disfigured and in desperate need of surgery. Now
with developments in 3D printing technology, a team of doctors has custom designed facial implants to specifically fit her face, allowing her a life
changing operation. But she’s not the only beneficiary. Carte Blanche explores this cutting-edge medical advancement

Script:


FINAL Script: 3D Face implants
8 July 2017
Duration: 10 minutes

Audio up: Claire walking into house and saying hello to Belinda

V/O Belinda Dzambo is a 32 year old mother and lives in Mayville, Durban where she shares the house with her sister Shingi and close relatives. They have been her support structure over the years and today she needs them more than ever as she prepares for a big operation in the morning.

Audio up: Belinda and Shingi kitchen making tea

V/O Seven years ago Belinda started developing a pain in her left lower jaw and went to the local clinic for help. They gave her pain tablets and said it would go away. For a while the medication helped but the swelling returned. Over time her face became more disfigured and sometimes painful. Then in November last year, out of desperation, she went to a local hospital where they diagnosed it as a tumour.

Claire Mawisa: What happened last year when they told you you had a growth? Did they explain what it meant to have a growth?
Belinda Dzambo: Patient: (Shona: sub-titles) All they say is that it is just a growth and if you don’t do something immediately it will spread throughout your face.
Claire Mawisa: How long have you been living with this growth?
Belinda Dzambo: (English - no subtitles) It is now 7 years.

V/O Belinda was then referred to Dr. Vivesh Rughubar, a specialist at the King Edward state hospital.

Claire Mawisa: When did you first meet Belina?
Dr. Vivesh Rughubar: Belinda was referred to us at King Edward from one of the outside hospitals that was early this year, and she came in complained of pain, discomfort and swelling. So it started out a process of radiographs, Xrays, a CT scan and a biopsy.
Claire Mawisa: And what did you find?
Dr. Vivesh Rughubar: Maxillofacial and oral surgeon: We found it was a benign tumour meaning it is not a cancerous tumour which is a slow growing locally invasive type of tumour.

V/O Dr. Rughubar then explained to Belinda that the growth on her left jaw was slowly disintegrating the jawbone. She would have to undergo an operation during which the tumour and part of the jawbone would be removed, and in its place they would put a 3D printed titanium medical implant.

Claire Mawisa: How did you feel when they said, Belinda you are going to get an operation?
Belinda Dzambo: (English - no subtitles) I am happy. (subtitles) I am going to be happy because my children think that I was born like this. They have never seen my normal face look normal.

Link: For Belinda a life changing experience is about to happen. Today is her last day of her tumour before she receives her 3D printed implant.

V/O Belinda is one of three state patients selected to undergo 3D medical implants at the Life Chatsmed Garden Hospital in Durban. The other two patients are Busisiwe Masuku and Sibusiso Nxumalo.

Up sound

V/O In each case the tumour will be removed and a 3d printed titanium medical implant will replace the disintegrated jawbone.

Busisiwe Masuku: 3D Implant Patient: (Zulu - subtitles) I sleep on the side, the right side. I am in pain and then pus, fluid also comes out at night. I cannot sleep well because (the fluid) just drips at night when I’m sleeping.

V/O For Busisiwe the discomfort became unbearable as the tumour started growing rapidly over the last few months.

Claire Mawisa: How do you feel now that you are having the operation?
Busisiwe Masuku: (Zulu - subtitles) I am very happy
Claire Mawisa: You’re not scared?
Busisiwe Masuku: (Zulu - subtitles) A little bit.
Claire Mawisa: it’s a beautiful thing that is happening in your life. I am excited for you. Tomorrow this time it will be gone.

V/O And as we left our patients that evening a few last words from the family brought comfort in anticipation for the big day ahead.

V/O Leading the way in modern 3D printing technology, is the Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing or CRPM at the Central University of Technology in Bloemfontein. Medical products are developed here to service an ever growing market. Vice Chancellor and Principal Henk de Jager is proud of the role the centre is playing.

Prof. Henk de Jager: Vice Chancellor and Principal: The production of medical products in this case where we have a strong focus on titanium custom made implants is absolutely crucial. It aligns with our vision of a strong focus on technological and social innovations and if you seen what CRPM is doing exactly is to make a difference in people’s lives.

V/O The centre is run by a small team of highly skilled engineers, designers and quality control staff. The first medical implants were printed at this centre in 2013 and it has since gained momentum. Gerrie Booysen heads up the team.

Gerrie Booysen: Director: CRPM: We assisted about 60 patients here in the last 3 years. Some of these patients actually lost their eye, nose, ear due to cancer or a disease. The need is still very high and we are trying to secure additional funding to help these patients.

V/O To print one titanium implant costs in the region of R80 000. The Fuchs Foundation sponsored the implants for these patients; the surgeons, the anaesthetist and theatre staff all offered their time at no cost and the hospital fees were wavered.

Audio up: Belinda being wheeled into

Link: We are standing by to join the team of surgeons and medical staff in the theatre where a three hour operation will give Belinda a new lease on life.

V/O During the next few hours the four weeks of hard work by a dedicated team of specialists from different cities will all come together. As the tumour is removed, the question remains, will the implant fit precisely?

Audio up: We are putting in the cutting guide.

V/O The tumour grows rapidly, so time is of the essence in the production process of the 3D printed implants. The whole process from start to finish takes 4 weeks. X Rays are taken of the patient’s jawbones on a CT scan and then sent to the centre in Bloemfontein where Johan Els converts the 2D images into a 3D model.

Johan Els: Programme Engineer: CRPM: A CT scan is 2 dimensional - a stack of images - and we have special software that can change that 2 dimensional images into a 3d model. That 3d model first of all is printed out for the surgeon as a planning model.

V/O The planning or test model, is printed in nylon, and this will become the working model to simulate the operation beforehand. Prof. Cules van den Heever, a prosthodontist from Pretoria forms the link between the surgeons in Durban and the design engineers in Bloemfontein. On the planning model they will indicate exactly where the tumour will be resected during the operation.

Prof. Cules van den Heever: Prosthodontist: I discuss the treatment plan and the resection lines with the surgeons and once we have the resection lines sorted out I go back to the design engineers and then we start with the designing of the custom implant.

V/O Once the final changes have been made to the working model it is time to start printing the final implant, this time in a high grade titanium which the body readily accepts. This process takes 42 hours.

UP music

V/O The titanium implants are then sent to the Central Analytical Facilities in Stellenbosch where the internal structure is examined to detect any cracks or voids present. Once it gets the green light, Titamed in Cape Town does the polishing of the implants to remove any rough edges. The final process is then sterilising the implant through gamma radiation at HEPRO in CapeTown.

Prof Culus van den Heever: You work off a CT scan and on a computer. This whole implant is designed and manufactured from computer data. The first time you see the patient is when you walk into theatre.

Johan Els: The main advantage of using this 3d printing technology is that it is customise patient specific implants. It is not an off the shelf component that you buy in various sizes and you are trying to make it fit.

Claire Mawisa: So what use to happed before the 3d printed implant?
Dr. Vivesh Rughubar: We use to take the patient to theatre, remove the tumour and then start bending the plate to adapt it to the opposite side but it wasn’t ideal. We always had problems and it took a long time.

Audio up: Where do you normally bite?

Claire Mawisa: So what are the benefits of having these custom designed implants?
Dr. Vivesh Rughubar: Shorter time; shorter anaesthetic time, which doesn't compromise the patient more and a better fit.

V/O Back in theatre, the moment everyone has been waiting for: Belinda will be receiving her custom designed implant unique to her features. Through the precision work of dr. Rughubar and the team the implant is screwed into place where the lower jaw use to be.

Up audio: And hopefully it will click into position like we anticipated. It fits like a glove.

Link: To the relief of all those involved, the implant fits like a glove. The operation was a success, and Belinda will be wheeled off to recovery shortly.

Up music: song

V/O When Belinda wakes up she will be happy to find the growth that has deformed her face for so many years, is finally gone. In a few days time Belinda will be back home with her family again.

Up music

V/O A few days after the operation we received a surprise a video clip of Belinda at home. She is still very sore and swollen but in time this too will pass and she will have her old smile back again.

Belinda Dzambo: (in English) Thank you. (she smiles)
_______________________________________________________________________
SUNDAY PROMO UNMIXED - 10 seconds:
We take you into the operating theatre to witness how 3D printed, custom designed medical implants are changing lives.
UP AUDIO: 4 Seconds
The main advantage of using this 3D printing technology is that it is customise patient specific implants.
30 SECOND VISUALS

10 SECOND PROMO MIXED
Through remarkable 3D printing technology, medical implants can now be custom-designed to replace damaged bone and match an individual’s own unique bone structure.

15 SECOND PROMO MIXED
V/O With technological advancements in 3D printing, implants of almost any part of the body can now be created at the push of a button.
Johan Els: The main advantage of using this 3d printing technology is that it is customise patient specific implants. So with this software you are designing for that specific patient.

15 SECOND PROMO
V/O 3D printing technology is rapidly changing the face of medicine.
Gerrie Booysen: We assisted around 60 patients here in the last 3 years.
V/O Custom designed facial implants are now giving patients new hope.

As the tumour is removed, the question remains, will the implant fit precisely? Audio up: We are putting in the cutting guide. V/O The tumour grows rapidly, so time is of the essence in the production process of the 3D printed implants. The whole process from start to finish takes 4 weeks. X Rays are taken of the patient’s jawbones on a CT scan and then sent to the centre in Bloemfontein where Johan Els converts the 2D images into a 3D model. Johan Els: Programme Engineer: CRPM: A CT scan is 2 dimensional - a stack of images - and we have special software that can change that 2 dimensional images into a 3d model. That 3d model first of all is printed out for the surgeon as a planning model. V/O The planning or test model, is printed in nylon, and this will become the working model to simulate the operation beforehand. Prof. Cules van den Heever, a prosthodontist from Pretoria forms the link between the surgeons in Durban and the design engineers in Bloemfontein. On the planning model they will indicate exactly where the tumour will be resected during the operation. Prof. Cules van den Heever: Prosthodontist: I discuss the treatment plan and the resection lines with the surgeons and once we have the resection lines sorted out I go back to the design engineers and then we start with the designing of the custom implant. V/O Once the final changes have been made to the working model it is time to start printing the final implant, this time in a high grade titanium which the body readily accepts. This process takes 42 hours. UP music V/O The titanium implants are then sent to the Central Analytical Facilities in Stellenbosch where the internal structure is examined to detect any cracks or voids present. Once it gets the green light, Titamed in Cape Town does the polishing of the implants to remove any rough edges. The final process is then sterilising the implant through gamma radiation at HEPRO in CapeTown. Prof Culus van den Heever: You work off a CT scan and on a computer. This whole implant is designed and manufactured from computer data. The first time you see the patient is when you walk into theatre. Johan Els: The main advantage of using this 3d printing technology is that it is customise patient specific implants. It is not an off the shelf component that you buy in various sizes and you are trying to make it fit. Claire Mawisa: So what use to happed before the 3d printed implant? Dr. Vivesh Rughubar: We use to take the patient to theatre, remove the tumour and then start bending the plate to adapt it to the opposite side but it wasn’t ideal. We always had problems and it took a long time. Audio up: Where do you normally bite? Claire Mawisa: So what are the benefits of having these custom designed implants? Dr. Vivesh Rughubar: Shorter time; shorter anaesthetic time, which doesn't compromise the patient more and a better fit. V/O Back in theatre, the moment everyone has been waiting for: Belinda will be receiving her custom designed implant unique to her features. Through the precision work of dr. Rughubar and the team the implant is screwed into place where the lower jaw use to be. Up audio: And hopefully it will click into position like we anticipated. It fits like a glove. Link: To the relief of all those involved, the implant fits like a glove. The operation was a success, and Belinda will be wheeled off to recovery shortly. Up music: song V/O When Belinda wakes up she will be happy to find the growth that has deformed her face for so many years, is finally gone. In a few days time Belinda will be back home with her family again. Up music V/O A few days after the operation we received a surprise a video clip of Belinda at home. She is still very sore and swollen but in time this too will pass and she will have her old smile back again. Belinda Dzambo: (in English) Thank you. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche: The medical world has been revolutionised through the help of 3D printing. Tonight we go to theatre to see how a team of experts perform miracles.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Through the revolutionary medical advances of safe 3D printed implants, patients are now able to leave surgery without any disfigurement of their facial features and lead a normal life.
metadata.Summary: Summary: Six years ago Belinda Dzambo from Mayville in Durban was diagnosed with a tumour of the jawbone. Over the years it became worst and eventually spread to the entire right hand side of her face. Bleeding, severe discomfort and disfigurement of her face has left her in despair. She was put on a waiting list at the state hospital for an operation that will remove the tumour but at the same time leave her with facial disfigurement. Reconstructive surgery after such an operation is the norm, but for Belinda this was not an option as state patients are not afforded that luxury. Then a few weeks ago she was contacted by Dr. Vivesh Rughubar, a maxillofacial surgeon from the King Edward state hospital in Durban with the good news. Through private funding and sponsorship her life was about to change.
metadata.Further information: We will visit Belinda at her home in Mayville where she lives with her sister, Shingi. Her two children are living in Zimbabwe with her mother as she has no means to look after them without a job. Her home language is Shona but we will converse with her through our Presenter, in Zulu. She has told us that she lives with pain and bleeding for too long. Her condition is desperate and she is thankful that she was chosen to receive the procedure free of charge. She hopes this is going to change her life as she is embarrassed about her disfigurement. At the same time she is nervous and scared and just hope that it will be a success. As a secondary case study 30 year old Busisiwe Masuku who lives in rural KZN will be interviewed at the hospital. This is not ideal as we do not see her home environment but her interview will be short. Background: In 2007 the Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) was established in Bloemfontein at the Central University of Technology (TUT) in the Free State. CRPM is considered one of the top centres in the world and the only one of its kind in the southern hemisphere. There are ten printing machines able to produce parts in titanium and a number of other materials for industries such as aerospace and architect and design and even jewelry in 3D printing. 3D printing, also called Additive Manufacturing, or AD is a process of joining materials layer upon layer until the final product or model is completed in the desired material. In this instance Belinda’s artificial jawbone was printed in titanium on the 3D printing machine to the exact specification of her facial features. In 2012 the first successful 3d implant in South Africa was successfully executed in Pretoria. Since then more than 30 state patients have been assisted through the help of private / public partnership where the medical team and hospital foot the bill and private funding sponsors the cost of the implant. Each implant costs roughly R70 000 to produce. Through this collaboration there is new hope for state patients in South Africa. The process involved from beginning to end is fascinating as it involves a team of experts working remotely from different corners of South Africa. In this instance, Dr, Rughubar sent CT scans of Belinda’s mandible to an engineer at the CRPM centre in Bloemfontein. This was captured through software on a computer and first printed in nylon as a test model. Due to the cost of titanium nylon is used as a dummy model. Once the team was satisfied with the fit and accuracy time was of an essence as the tumour keeps on growing and every month Belinda’s jaw area will start looking different. Two weeks prior to the operation, the final product was then printed in titanium and sent to Stellenbosch to be checked that there are no cracks in the model. From there it went to Cape Town to the Titamed centre where the product is polished and then finally treated by a radioactive material to ensure that there will be no infection in the patient after the surgery. The advantages of 3D printed medical implants are that they are safe; save on hospital and recovery time and that the patients is able to lead a life of normality thanks to the perfect fit of the titanium printed model. Without the 3D printed implant the patient would have to undergo up to nine hours surgery, then ICU, then a lengthy recovery period. They are then sent home disfigured as reconstructive surgery is not affordable. Besides the engineer in charge of the printing we will also interview the medical expert at the hospital performing the operation and hopefully will be allowed to film inside the theatre. The programme will conclude with Belinda out of theatre and wheeled to her hospital bed where we will hopefully get a thumbs up from her to show that it went well.
